subject: ss-medical-oncology
title: Febrile neutropenia, fungal markers and catheter infection

steps.tx: **Neutrophil kinetics** (the rate at which these cells are made and lost) decides how chemotherapy-induced neutropenia (a low neutrophil count caused by treatment) unfolds. Mature neutrophils survive about 12 hours in blood and about 3 days in tissue. A reserve of mature granulocytes in the blood-forming tissue lasts about 7 days. Progenitors need 10 to 14 days to mature, so the **nadir** (lowest point of the count) falls near day 10 and recovery completes by day 21.
steps.say: Neutrophil kinetics, meaning how quickly these cells are made and lost, decides how chemotherapy-induced neutropenia unfolds. Mature neutrophils have a working life of roughly 12 hours in the bloodstream and about 3 days once they enter tissue. Mature granulocytes held in the blood-forming tissue can cover about 7 days of demand. Progenitor cells need 10 to 14 days to mature, so the count usually bottoms out near day 10. Recovery is complete by day 21.

steps.tx: Hematopoietic growth factors (signals that drive blood cell production) include **filgrastim**, a recombinant (genetically engineered) granulocyte colony-stimulating factor (G-CSF) that prolongs neutrophil survival. **Sargramostim** is the only recombinant granulocyte-macrophage colony-stimulating factor (GM-CSF) approved in the United States. **Oprelvekin**, recombinant interleukin-11 (IL-11), was approved to ease low platelet counts but was withdrawn for weak effect and substantial toxicity.
steps.say: Several hematopoietic growth factors stimulate blood cell production. Filgrastim is a genetically engineered form of granulocyte colony-stimulating factor, and it helps neutrophils survive longer. Sargramostim is the only engineered granulocyte-macrophage colony-stimulating factor approved in the United States. Oprelvekin once eased low platelet counts, but regulators withdrew it because it worked poorly and caused significant toxicity.

rows: Only approved recombinant GM-CSF in the United States

steps.tx: The **Multinational Association of Supportive Care in Cancer (MASCC)** risk index sorts patients with a risk of neutropenic infection into high and low risk groups by adding points. A total of 21 or higher is low risk, while a total below 21 is high risk. Absence of hypotension (low blood pressure) adds 5 points, outpatient status adds 3, and age under 60 years adds 2.
steps.say: The Multinational Association of Supportive Care in Cancer risk index, usually called MASCC, places each patient into a high or low risk group. Points are added for several features. Having no low blood pressure earns 5 points, and being an outpatient earns 3. Being under 60 years old earns 2 more. A total of 21 or higher is low risk, while a total below 21 is high risk.

steps.tx: **Febrile neutropenia** (fever with a low neutrophil count) means one oral reading of 38.3 degrees Celsius, or 38.0 degrees held for 1 hour, with a neutrophil count below 500 per microlitre. **Empirical** antibiotics (chosen before any germ is identified) ideally begin within 1 hour of onset. Hypotension or signs of organ injury mark clinical instability and call for a broader regimen given intravenously.
steps.say: Febrile neutropenia means fever occurring alongside a low neutrophil count. A single oral reading of 38.3 degrees Celsius counts, as does 38.0 degrees held for an hour. The neutrophil count must sit below 500 per microlitre. Antibiotics chosen before any germ is identified should start within an hour. Low blood pressure or signs of organ injury need a broader intravenous regimen.

nodes.label: Fever of 38.3 degrees Celsius with neutrophils below 500 per microlitre
Stable, lower risk: oral outpatient therapy may be considered
Hypotension or organ injury: broader regimen

steps.tx: **Pseudomonas aeruginosa** (a gram-negative bacterium) is the pathogen that empirical therapy must cover. Bacteremia (bacteria in the blood) during neutropenic fever carries much higher mortality, particularly gram-negative bacteremia. Single-agent options best studied for this purpose include **piperacillin-tazobactam**, **cefepime**, **ceftazidime**, **imipenem**, and **meropenem**. **Ceftriaxone** is absent from that list.
steps.say: Pseudomonas aeruginosa is a gram-negative bacterium that the first antibiotic needs to cover. Bloodstream infections during neutropenic fever carry high mortality, especially those caused by gram-negative organisms. The best-studied single agents include piperacillin-tazobactam, cefepime, ceftazidime, imipenem, and meropenem. Ceftriaxone does not appear on that list of options.

left.title: Why Pseudomonas matters
points: Gram-negative bacterium that empirical therapy must cover
Gram-negative bacteremia carries particularly high mortality

steps.tx: Routine **vancomycin** is not part of the starting regimen, because adding it routinely brings more nephrotoxicity (kidney injury) without better outcomes. Gram-positive cover is added for specific reasons: sepsis, clinically evident soft tissue infection, suspected catheter exit site infection, pneumonia, severe mucositis when ceftazidime is the starting agent, or known carriage of methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA).
steps.say: Vancomycin is not added routinely to the first antibiotic plan. Routine use has not improved outcomes, and it does add kidney toxicity. It is used only in particular situations. Those include sepsis, a clear soft tissue infection, a suspected catheter exit site infection, and pneumonia. Severe mucositis qualifies only when ceftazidime is the starting agent. Known carriage of methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus also qualifies.

rows: Sepsis or clinically evident soft tissue infection
Add only if ceftazidime is the starting agent

steps.tx: The **galactomannan** test, most useful on bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) fluid, helps diagnose aspergillosis, but false negatives are common in patients on antifungal prophylaxis (preventive drugs). The **beta-D-glucan** (BDG) test has a high negative predictive value for invasive candidiasis, meaning a negative result makes that infection unlikely, yet it lacks specificity. Biomarker results are listed as negative in mucormycosis.
steps.say: Two fungal tests come up often. Galactomannan is most useful when run on bronchoalveolar lavage fluid for aspergillosis. Results can be falsely negative in patients taking preventive antifungal drugs. Beta-D-glucan has a strong negative predictive value for invasive candidiasis, so a negative result makes that infection less likely. However, it does not reliably identify the specific cause of a positive result. Biomarkers come back negative in mucormycosis.

left.title: Galactomannan
points: Most useful on lavage fluid for aspergillosis
False negatives common with antifungal prophylaxis
False positives can occur with other fungal infections

right.title: Beta-D-glucan (BDG)
points: High negative predictive value for invasive candidiasis

steps.tx: **Catheter-related bacteremia** (blood infection tied to an indwelling line) is supported when the same organism grows from both a central line culture and a peripheral vein culture. The **differential time to positivity** (the gap before each culture flags growth) points to the catheter when the central culture turns positive at least 2 hours earlier. Once confirmed, the preferred step is removing the catheter.
steps.say: Catheter-related bacteremia means germs in the blood traced back to an indwelling line. Doctors confirm it when the same organism grows from both a central line culture and a peripheral vein culture. The timing helps as well. If the central culture turns positive at least 2 hours earlier, the catheter is the likely source. Once confirmed, the preferred step is to remove the catheter.

nodes.label: Same organism grows from central line and peripheral vein
Central culture turns positive at least 2 hours earlier
